common_name: Pesto Besto Basil (Proven Winners Downy Mildew-Resistant Sweet Italian Basil)

planting.note: Set out started plants after all danger of frost has passed; Pesto Besto is a vegetatively propagated hybrid sold as starts rather than seed, and reaches usable harvest size within 4-6 weeks of transplanting from a 4-inch container.

directions: Pesto Besto is a Proven Winners sweet Italian basil bred to stay productive for foliage far longer than seed-grown Genovese types, since it is notably late to flower and sets little to no seed. Removing any sporadic flower spikes that do appear keeps the plant channeling energy into fresh, deliciously aromatic leaf production for pesto and other classic Italian preparations. It carries strong resistance to downy mildew, a disease that quickly ruins many basil plantings, and won a Top Performer award in University of Guelph trials. Grow in full sun with average soil fertility and even moisture, and expect an upright, well-filled habit that works equally well as a container thriller or a garden bed herb.
sources: Proven Winners — Pesto Besto plant profile (provenwinners.com)
University of Guelph Trial Garden — 2021 Top Performer recognition

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in full sun; Ajaka is part of the German-bred Herbalea basil series and is propagated from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Ajaka is a tall, well-branched selection from the Herbalea basil breeding program in Germany, with bright green, elliptic leaves and a sweet-spicy, distinctly spicy-tasting flavor. From late June through September it produces roughly a hundred and fifty small reddish-purple flower spikes that draw pollinators while the plant continues producing harvestable foliage. It tolerates cool, rainy nights down into the mid-40s Fahrenheit noticeably better than standard seed-grown basil and shows good tolerance of Fusarium, Botrytis, and Pythium. Use it as a dual-purpose container or border plant, harvesting leaves for cooking while letting some flower spikes develop for ornamental and pollinator value.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP24587 (Herbalea GmbH) — Google Patents

common_name: Habana Basil (Herbalea Cool-Tolerant High-Yield Ornamental Basil)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost; Habana is bred for improved cool-temperature tolerance compared with standard seed-grown basil, letting it be set out a bit earlier or extend later into fall.

directions: Habana, from the Herbalea breeding series, is valued for its tall habit and exceptionally high leaf production compared with everyday sweet basil. Its standout trait is improved tolerance of cool nights, which keeps leaf production going later into a cool fall or through a chilly spring than most seed-grown culinary basils can manage. The abundant green foliage carries the classic sweet basil aroma and flavor, making frequent harvest for cooking easy without quickly exhausting the plant. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture, and pinch stem tips periodically to keep the vigorous habit full and bushy.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP24643 (Herbalea GmbH) — Google Patents

common_name: Dark Lady Basil (Herbalea Deep-Purple Ornamental Basil)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in full sun; Dark Lady is also sold under the trade name Fairytale Dark Lady by some retailers.

directions: Dark Lady is a Herbalea-series basil selected for its striking foliage, broadly ovate leaves colored deep purple-violet on top with a nearly blackish-violet underside and prominent contrasting veins. The tall, well-branched habit and sweet-spicy, aromatic flavor make it as useful in the kitchen as it is dramatic in a border or container planting, where its dark coloring contrasts well with green-leaved herbs and flowers. It tolerates cool, rainy nights better than typical seed-grown purple basils and shows good tolerance of common basil fungal diseases. Harvest leaves regularly to encourage continued branching and to keep the deep color at its most vivid on new growth.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP24644 (Herbalea GmbH) — Google Patents

common_name: Green Ball Basil (Herbalea Non-Flowering Dwarf Globe Basil)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost; Green Ball never flowers, so no pinching is needed to delay bolting or preserve leaf flavor.

directions: Green Ball is an extremely compact, naturally rounded basil from the Herbalea breeding series, forming a dense little globe only a few inches tall from dozens of branches packed with small, uniformly green lanceolate leaves. Because it is non-flowering and sets no seed, it never turns bitter or bolts the way standard basil does once it blooms, so every leaf stays tender and mildly sweet-spicy for the entire season. It tolerates cool, rainy nights noticeably better than ordinary sweet basil and resists common basil fungal problems. Its tight, self-shaping habit makes it ideal for edging, small pots, or window boxes where a globe basil like Spicy Globe is traditionally used, with an even denser, more uniform shape.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP24615 (Herbalea GmbH) — Google Patents

common_name: Green Fortune Basil (Herbalea Spicy Cold-Tolerant Ornamental Basil)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in full sun; Green Fortune is bred for cool-night tolerance and heavy bloom production.

directions: Green Fortune is a tall, well-branched, rounded Herbalea-series basil with glossy green elliptic leaves and a notably spicy flavor and aroma. From late June through September it produces an abundance of small purple-and-white flower spikes, prized by pollinators, while the stems themselves shift from yellow-green at the base to violet toward the tips for added seasonal interest. It tolerates cool, rainy nights significantly better than typical seed-grown basil and shows good resistance to Fusarium and Botrytis. Grow it in full sun as a productive culinary herb or let it flower heavily as an ornamental pollinator plant in a border or large container.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent PP24471 (Herbalea GmbH) — Google Patents

common_name: Wild Color Basil (Herbalea Green-and-Purple Ornamental Basil)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in full sun; Wild Color is grown as an annual or short-lived perennial depending on climate.

directions: Wild Color is a Herbalea-series basil with an upright habit and leaves that mix green and purple for a variegated, eye-catching effect, topped in summer with purple flower spikes that keep bees busy all season. It is highly aromatic and flavorful, equally suited to slicing fresh for a caprese salad or working into pesto. Like other members of the Herbalea line, it shows better weather resistance and disease tolerance than typical seed-grown basil. Grow in full sun with moderate, even watering in containers or garden borders, pinching occasionally to keep the compact habit full.

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in full sun; Lhasa is part of the Herbalea basil series bred for combined ornamental and culinary performance.

directions: Lhasa is a robust, well-branched Herbalea-series basil prized for combining strong culinary performance with garden presence, forming a dense mound that spreads wider than it grows tall. Its foliage is very fragrant with a notably strong basil taste, making it a reliable choice for cooks who also want an attractively full container or border plant. Like its Herbalea siblings, it benefits from regular harvesting, which keeps the dense, well-filled habit looking its best through the season. Grow in full sun with even moisture; in zones 9-11 it can persist as a short-lived perennial, while elsewhere it is grown as a warm-season annual from purchased starts.
